## Frequently asked questions

### What's the best European country for an American retiree in 2026?

Portugal is the default starting point in this shortlist for retirees assessing passive-income residence. The best individual choice depends on residence eligibility, finances, healthcare and housing; no country wins for every household.

### Is Portugal better than Spain for American retirees?

Portugal and Spain fit different residence-planning questions. Portugal's D7 route is a starting point for qualifying passive-income applicants, while Spain's non-lucrative route is relevant to a nonworking retirement plan. Have an immigration professional assess your circumstances before choosing.

### Can I retire in Europe using only tourist permission?

Tourist permission is not long-term residence permission. For U.S. visitors, the standard Schengen short-stay allowance is up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen area, not a fresh allowance in each country. Long-term retirement requires the appropriate residence route.

### Will Medicare cover my healthcare after I move to Europe?

Medicare generally does not cover healthcare outside the United States, with limited exceptions. Arrange appropriate overseas coverage and verify any public-system eligibility before departure. Prescription continuity needs its own plan.

### Do Americans still file U.S. taxes after retiring abroad?

U.S. citizens generally remain subject to U.S. tax rules on worldwide income while living abroad. Filing requirements depend on individual circumstances, and foreign account reporting can also apply. A qualified cross-border tax professional should assess both countries' obligations.

### Should I buy a home before applying for retirement residence?

Do not make a property purchase your first step. Establish residence eligibility and accommodation-evidence requirements, then obtain local contract advice before committing. Property ownership and permission to reside are separate questions.

### Can Global Systems Studio handle my immigration and tax decisions?

Global Systems Studio provides destination-independent relocation coaching and consulting through ROS™, not individualized legal, tax or investment advice. ROS™ can coordinate the planning sequence; qualified specialists must answer the regulated professional questions.

## Best golden visa programs for Americans relocating abroad in 2026
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/best-golden-visa-programs-americans-relocating-abroad-2026/

Best overall for property-based residence with no stay requirement: Greece. Best for a low physical-presence route: Portugal. Best for entrepreneurs: Italy. The best golden visa programs for Americans in 2026 are the ones where the investment, the residence rules and your actual life plan fit together, not the ones with the lowest headline number.

## TL;DR

- Spain closed its golden visa to new applicants in April 2025, and Portugal ended its real estate route in 2023, so older lists that still feature them are out of date.
- Greece, Portugal, Italy, Cyprus and Malta remain the programs most often discussed for Americans, but thresholds and rules change; confirm current figures with an immigration professional.
- A golden visa is a residence permit, not a tax plan. As a U.S. citizen you generally keep U.S. filing obligations wherever you live.
- Decide why you want residence first (access, flexibility, a retirement base) and only then choose a program.

## Why this matters

Investment residence feels simple: invest, receive a permit. In practice it ties a large, hard-to-reverse financial commitment to an immigration outcome. If the program changes, closes or turns out not to fit your plans, the money does not come back automatically.

Global Systems Studio is best for Americans who need that decision sequenced alongside legal, tax, housing and healthcare planning. Its ROS™ coaching and consulting system coordinates those workstreams without replacing regulated advice. The Global Systems Studio site introduces that planning approach.

Treat this list as a pressure test for a shortlist you are building, not as a recommendation to invest. Industry sources describe thresholds that shift from year to year, and several well-known programs have already closed.

## What makes a golden visa worth considering?

The ranking uses practical planning criteria rather than a claim that one program suits every American.

- Program status: Confirm the program is open to new applicants today, not just listed on an older comparison.
- Investment type: Property, funds, businesses and donations carry different risks, costs and exit options.
- Physical presence: Some routes ask for little time in the country; others expect more. Match this to how you actually want to live.
- Path beyond the permit: Ask whether the permit can lead to long-term residence or citizenship and what that would require.
- Tax coordination: Residence permission does not settle U.S. filing obligations or local tax residence. Assess them separately.
- Family and dependants: Check who can be included and what documents each person needs.

## At a glance

Country | Best for | Standout planning advantage | Key limitation |

Greece | Property-based residence without a stay requirement | Zone-based property thresholds introduced in 2024 | Thresholds vary by location and have changed before |

Portugal | A low physical-presence route | Fund and cultural routes remain after the real estate route ended | Investment must fit a narrower set of routes |

Italy | Entrepreneurs and founders | Routes built around startups and companies | Requires a real business plan, not a passive purchase |

Cyprus | Property buyers who can show steady income | A defined property-based route | Income evidence and periodic presence are expected |

Malta | A lower-commitment residence route | A residency program that continues after citizenship by investment ended | Lower entry cost does not mean lower scrutiny |

These are use-case recommendations, not promises of approval, low taxes or affordable care. Figures are as reported by industry sources in 2026 and change often, so confirm them with the official authority.

## 1. Greece: best for property-based residence

Greece is the program most often discussed by Americans who want a residence permit tied to property. Since a 2024 overhaul, industry sources describe zone-based thresholds, with higher amounts in the most in-demand areas and lower amounts elsewhere. Reported figures have ranged from roughly 250,000 to 800,000 euros depending on location and property type.

Confirm which zone your property falls in and whether the type of property you have in mind qualifies. Rules on short-term rentals and renovation have also changed in recent years, so do not assume that last year's guidance still applies.

Pros:

- A property route gives you something tangible to hold.
- Sources describe no minimum stay requirement for holding the permit.
- Zone-based pricing offers lower-cost areas to evaluate.

Cons:

- Thresholds and eligible property types have changed more than once.
- Property carries purchase costs, taxes and exit risk beyond the permit itself.
- Local tax residence is a separate question from holding the permit.

Best for: Americans who want a European property base and can commit capital for the long term.

Verdict: Confirm the zone, the property type and the current threshold in writing before you sign anything.

## 2. Portugal: best for a low physical-presence route

Portugal ended its real estate route in 2023, which is why older golden visa lists mislead. Fund-based and cultural or artistic contribution routes are still reported as available, with industry sources citing figures around 500,000 euros for funds and 250,000 euros for cultural contributions.

The route is associated with a short annual presence requirement, but that is only the permit rule. If you intend to live there, residence, tax and housing decisions still need their own assessment.

Pros:

- Industry sources describe a very short annual presence requirement.
- Funds and contributions avoid owning and managing property.
- The permit can be part of a longer residence timeline, subject to current rules.

Cons:

- The real estate route is closed, so many popular guides are outdated.
- Fund investments carry market risk and fees.
- A permit that asks for little presence does not build your daily-life foundation by itself.

Best for: Americans who want access to a European residence permit without relocating full time.

Verdict: Treat the fund as an investment decision first and a visa decision second.

## 3. Italy: best for entrepreneurs

Italy's investor routes are better suited to people who plan to build or back a business than to passive buyers. Industry sources describe lower thresholds for startup investment and higher ones for established companies, with processing that can be relatively quick compared with some alternatives.

Because the route expects real activity, the application is only as strong as the plan behind it. Ask a qualified Italian immigration professional what documentation the authority expects for your specific structure.

Pros:

- Routes are built around startups and companies rather than property.
- Reported processing times can be shorter than some other programs.
- Italy offers a base for founders who want a European market presence.

Cons:

- A genuine business plan is expected.
- Business investment risk sits with you.
- Italian tax and corporate rules add complexity that a visa guide cannot cover.

Best for: Founders and investors who want a European operating base.

Verdict: Skip this route if you want a passive property purchase.

## 4. Cyprus: best for property buyers with steady income

Cyprus offers a property-based residence route that industry sources describe with a purchase threshold in the region of 300,000 euros, along with an expectation of reliable annual income and periodic presence in the country.

That combination suits buyers who already have dependable income and who expect to visit regularly. It fits less well if you want a purely passive permit or if your income is irregular.

Pros:

- A defined property-based route is available.
- Periodic presence is reported as modest compared with full-time residence.
- The income expectation encourages an honest budget from the start.

Cons:

- Income evidence adds a documentation burden.
- Property carries purchase costs and exit risk.
- Permit conditions can change, so confirm them with the authority or a specialist.

Best for: Americans with stable income who want a Mediterranean property base.

Verdict: Document your income before you commit to a purchase.

## 5. Malta: best for a lower-commitment residence route

Malta's citizenship by investment ended in 2025, but its residency program continues. Industry sources describe a leasing option with a relatively low entry figure, reported around 150,000 euros, alongside other qualifying routes.

A lower entry cost does not mean lighter due diligence. Expect background checks and ask what ongoing conditions apply to renewal.

Pros:

- Residency continues even though citizenship by investment closed.
- A leasing route reduces upfront capital compared with a purchase.
- English is widely used in everyday administration.

Cons:

- Due diligence can be thorough.
- Renewal conditions need to be understood up front.
- The program is not a route to citizenship.

Best for: Americans who want a European residence permit with a smaller capital commitment.

Verdict: Ask what renewal requires before you treat the low entry figure as the whole cost.

## How this shortlist is ranked

Greece leads for property-based residence, Portugal for a low physical-presence route, Italy for entrepreneurs, Cyprus for buyers with steady income and Malta for a smaller capital commitment.

The order does not establish comparative returns, tax outcomes or approval likelihood. Use it to choose your next investigation, not to authorize an investment.

Organize four workstreams: legal, financial, housing and healthcare. Keep them in one dependency list so that a requirement in one area does not disappear inside another professional's brief.

### Program eligibility

Confirm the program is open, the threshold and investment type, and the documents each family member needs. Identify anything needing translation or an apostille before you order document services.

### Financial review

Decide how the investment is funded and what it does to your liquidity. Ask a cross-border tax professional about U.S. reporting for foreign property, funds or entities, including foreign account and asset reporting rules.

### Housing and presence

Match your presence plan to the permit. A permit that needs little time in the country can still sit alongside a lease or purchase that assumes you will be there.

### Healthcare bridge

Residence permission does not arrange coverage. Document how you will obtain care while you hold the permit, and do not assume Medicare covers routine care abroad.

Prepare two cash-flow scenarios: investment completed on schedule and investment delayed. These are planning suggestions, not program requirements. ## Frequently asked questions

### Is Spain's golden visa still available in 2026?

No. Spain ended its golden visa for new applicants in April 2025. Guides that still list it are out of date, so confirm current options with an immigration professional.

### Can Americans still get a Portuguese golden visa in 2026?

The real estate route ended in 2023, but fund-based and cultural contribution routes are reported as available. Confirm current rules and thresholds before you plan around them.

### Does a golden visa make me a citizen?

No. A golden visa is a residence permit. Citizenship is a separate process with its own requirements, and not every program leads to it.

### Do I still file U.S. taxes if I get a golden visa?

U.S. citizens generally remain subject to U.S. tax filing rules wherever they live. A residence permit does not change that, so get cross-border tax advice before you invest.

### How much does a golden visa cost?

It depends on the country, route and location, and figures change. Beyond the investment itself, budget for legal fees, taxes, due diligence and any ongoing costs.

### Can a golden visa replace a retirement or remote-work visa?

Sometimes, but not automatically. Compare what each route requires in terms of presence, income and activity before choosing the one that fits your plan.

### Can relocation coaching replace an immigration lawyer?

No. Global Systems Studio's ROS™ relocation coaching coordinates planning decisions; qualified immigration, tax and financial professionals provide advice within their respective regulated fields.

## One last thing

Before you commit to an investment, write down how you would exit it. Ask what happens if the program closes, if the property does not sell or if the fund underperforms.

For a 2026 plan, the best program is the one whose answers fit your residence, tax and family plan. Choose the purpose. Then build the sequence.

## Best international health insurance plans for US expats 2026
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/best-international-health-insurance-plans-us-expats-2026/

Best overall for most long-term expats: a comprehensive international private medical plan. Best for controlling cost: a plan that excludes the United States. Best once you have residency: local private or public cover. The best international health insurance plan for a US expat in 2026 is the one that matches where you will actually live, where you may need care and how much the United States has to be part of the picture.

## TL;DR

- Medicare generally does not pay for routine care abroad, and US marketplace plans are built around US residence, so most expats need a separate plan.
- The biggest price lever is the coverage area. Including the United States can raise premiums sharply, so decide whether you really need it.
- Pre-existing conditions, waiting periods, renewal terms and evacuation cover decide whether a plan holds up when you use it.
- Insurer names in this article are examples of the plan type, not endorsements. Check current terms with a licensed broker or the insurer.

## Why this matters

Healthcare is the item that most often turns a smooth move into an expensive one. A plan that looks fine on the quote page can exclude the condition you are most likely to claim for, or leave you uncovered during a waiting period at the exact moment you arrive.

Global Systems Studio is best for Americans who need the insurance decision sequenced with visas, housing and tax. Its ROS™ coaching and consulting system coordinates those workstreams without replacing licensed advice. The Global Systems Studio site introduces that planning approach. Global Systems Studio does not sell insurance.

Treat this list as a way to build a shortlist, not a recommendation to buy any product. Premiums, benefits and eligibility change by age, country and insurer.

## What should you check before choosing?

The ranking uses planning criteria rather than a claim that one plan fits every American.

- Coverage area: Worldwide with the United States and worldwide without it are very different products with very different prices.
- Pre-existing conditions: Ask whether the insurer reviews your history up front or applies a moratorium, and what each means for a later claim.
- Waiting periods: Maternity, dental and some treatments often carry waits before cover starts.
- Evacuation and repatriation: Confirm whether medical evacuation is included or sold separately.
- Direct billing and claims: Check how hospitals are paid and what you must pay up front.
- Renewal and residency rules: Some plans change terms with age or require you to live outside certain countries.

## At a glance

Plan type | Best for | Standout advantage | Key limitation |

International private medical | Long-term expats who move between countries | Broad network and evacuation options | Premiums rise with age and with US coverage |

Worldwide excluding the US | Cost-conscious expats who will not seek care at home | Meaningfully lower premiums in many cases | US treatment is not covered |

Local private insurance | Settled residents with a local address | Often cheaper, set up for local providers | May not travel with you if you move |

Local public system | Residents who qualify for enrollment | Low or income-linked cost in some countries | Eligibility, waiting times and contribution rules vary |

Employer or group expat plan | Employees sent abroad by a company | Group terms and employer handling of claims | Ends if the job ends |

These are use-case recommendations, not promises of coverage or price. Plan details change often, so confirm them with the insurer or a licensed broker.

## 1. International private medical insurance: best for most long-term expats

Comprehensive international plans are built for people who live outside their home country and may move again. Insurers such as Cigna Global, Allianz Care, Aetna International, GeoBlue and Bupa Global are commonly cited examples of this category.

The strength is portability and breadth. The trade-off is cost, and the details of underwriting. Read how pre-existing conditions are handled before you compare premiums.

Pros:

- Designed for people who live abroad rather than travel.
- Typically offers choices of deductible, coverage area and add-ons.
- Can include evacuation and a wide hospital network.

Cons:

- Premiums usually rise with age and with US coverage.
- Underwriting rules can exclude existing conditions.
- Some plans limit how long you can stay in the United States.

Best for: Americans who expect to live in more than one country or want one plan that travels.

Verdict: Get the pre-existing condition rules in writing before you pay.

## 2. Worldwide plans that exclude the United States: best for controlling cost

Many insurers offer the same plan with and without US coverage. Leaving the United States out is the single most common way expats lower their premium.

It only works if you are honest about how often you will be home. A planned visit, a family emergency or a medical crisis during a trip are the moments this choice gets tested.

Pros:

- Lower premium for similar benefits elsewhere.
- Simple to understand once you pick the coverage area.
- Pairs well with a separate travel plan for US trips.

Cons:

- No cover for US treatment.
- A long visit home may need a separate short-term policy.
- Returning to US residence changes your options.

Best for: Expats who live abroad full time and rarely return to the United States.

Verdict: Price the US-inclusive version once so you know what you are choosing to give up.

## 3. Local private insurance: best once you are settled

After you have a residence address and a visa, local private insurance is often more affordable and better aligned with local providers. Some visa categories require specific private cover, and the rules can be exact about what qualifies.

Local plans tend to be designed for residents, so they may not follow you if you move country or spend long periods elsewhere.

Pros:

- Often priced for local residents rather than expats.
- Can satisfy visa insurance requirements when it meets the stated criteria.
- Local claims handling and language.

Cons:

- May not travel with you.
- Pre-existing condition and age rules still apply.
- You need a local address and often a residence permit first.

Best for: Americans with residency who plan to stay in one country.

Verdict: Check the visa insurance rules before you buy, not after.

## 4. Local public healthcare: best where residents qualify

Several countries let legal residents join a public system, sometimes through contributions or a residence-linked fee. Eligibility, waiting periods and what is covered differ by country and visa type.

Public cover can be a strong base layer, and some expats add a private plan for faster access or for cover while travelling.

Pros:

- Can be low cost relative to private insurance.
- Gives access to the national system.
- Can be combined with private cover.

Cons:

- Enrollment rules are specific and may not apply to new arrivals right away.
- You may need cover for the gap before eligibility starts.
- Waiting times and access vary.

Best for: Long-term residents who meet their country's enrollment rules.

Verdict: Ask the national health authority what applies to your visa category, not a general forum.

## 5. Employer or group expat plans: best for company assignments

If a company sends you abroad, it may provide group health cover as part of the assignment. These plans often come with employer-managed claims and clearer terms.

The risk is the end date. When the assignment or job ends, so does the cover, and you may face underwriting again.

Pros:

- Employer handles enrollment and often claims.
- Group terms can be more forgiving than individual underwriting.
- May include family members.

Cons:

- Tied to the job.
- Individual cover may be harder to get later.
- Terms are set by the employer, not by you.

Best for: Employees on a defined overseas assignment.

Verdict: Ask what happens to your cover and your family's cover on the day the assignment ends.

## How this shortlist is ranked

International private medical plans lead for flexibility, ex-US worldwide plans for cost control, local private cover for settled residents, local public systems for qualifying residents and employer plans for assignments.

The order does not establish comparative price, claim performance or approval likelihood. Use it to decide what to investigate next, not to buy.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Medicare cover me if I live abroad?

Original Medicare generally does not cover routine care outside the United States. Check current rules with Medicare or a licensed advisor before you rely on it.

### Do I need international insurance if my destination has public healthcare?

Not always, but public access can depend on residence status and waiting periods. Many expats cover the gap or add private cover for faster access.

### What is the difference between a US plan and an international plan?

US marketplace plans are built around US residence and networks. International plans are built for people who live outside their home country and may include evacuation and cover in several countries.

### Why is including the United States so much more expensive?

US medical costs are high, so insurers price US coverage accordingly. Excluding it is a common way to lower premiums, at the cost of no US cover.

### Will an international plan cover pre-existing conditions?

It depends on the insurer and how it underwrites. Some review your history and may exclude conditions; others use a moratorium. Ask for the terms in writing.

### Is travel insurance enough for living abroad?

Usually not. Travel policies are designed for trips, not residence, and often have stay limits and narrower benefits.

## Best US expat tax preparation services in 2026
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/best-us-expat-tax-preparation-services-2026/

Best overall for most Americans abroad: a specialist expat tax firm staffed by CPAs or enrolled agents. Best for complex situations: an independent CPA or enrolled agent with international clients. Best for simple returns: expat-focused software. The best US expat tax preparation service in 2026 is the one that matches how complicated your foreign income, accounts and entities are.

## TL;DR

- US citizens generally file US returns wherever they live, even when they owe no US tax, so choosing a preparer who handles foreign income and reporting matters.
- Foreign account and asset reporting can apply separately from the return. FBAR is generally triggered when foreign accounts together exceed 10,000 US dollars at any time in the year.
- Simple situations can suit software. Business ownership, foreign pensions, late filing or past gaps usually call for a credentialed professional.
- Provider types are compared by problem solved, not ranked by brand. Check credentials and current IRS guidance before you hire.

## Why this matters

Expat tax mistakes are rarely loud. They show up as a missed form, a wrong exclusion choice or a foreign account nobody reported, and the cost can arrive years later as penalties and amended returns.

Global Systems Studio is best for Americans who need the tax decision sequenced alongside visas, banking and housing. Its ROS™ coaching and consulting system coordinates those workstreams without replacing regulated tax advice. The Global Systems Studio site introduces that planning approach.

Treat this list as a shortlist builder, not a recommendation to hire any firm. Tax rules, thresholds and deadlines change, so confirm current figures with the IRS or a qualified professional.

## What should you check before choosing?

The ranking uses practical planning criteria rather than a claim that one service suits every American.

- Credentials: Look for a CPA, enrolled agent or tax attorney, and ask who actually signs the return.
- Expat experience: Ask how many returns with foreign income, foreign accounts and foreign entities they prepare each year.
- Reporting scope: Confirm they handle FBAR and, where relevant, Form 8938, not just the income tax return.
- Representation: If the IRS writes to you, check whether the preparer is authorized to represent you.
- Late or past filings: Ask whether they help with catching up on earlier years and which IRS procedures may apply.
- Pricing clarity: Compare fees for the return, the foreign reporting and any state filing.

## At a glance

Provider type | Best for | Standout advantage | Key limitation |

Tax attorney | Penalty exposure or serious compliance issues | Legal privilege and representation | Typically the highest cost |

These are use-case recommendations, not promises of lower tax or fewer penalties. Confirm current rules, thresholds and deadlines with the IRS or a qualified professional.

## 1. Specialist expat tax firms: best for most Americans abroad

Firms that focus on US citizens abroad prepare returns with foreign income, the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, the foreign tax credit and foreign account reporting every day. That repetition is the main benefit.

Ask who prepares and who reviews. A firm is only as good as the credentialed person who signs.

Pros:

- Built for the forms and choices expats face.
- Usually handles FBAR and related reporting alongside the return.
- Often experienced with late filers.

Cons:

- Fees can exceed general software.
- Service quality varies by firm.
- Planning advice may be limited to the return itself.

Best for: Americans with foreign income or foreign accounts who want a dependable annual process.

Verdict: Confirm credentials and scope in writing before you send documents.

## 2. Independent CPAs or enrolled agents with international clients: best for complex situations

If you own a foreign company, have a foreign pension, hold rental property abroad or move between countries, a credentialed independent can tailor advice to your facts.

The quality of this option depends on the individual. Ask for examples of the situations they handle and how they stay current on rules for Americans abroad.

Pros:

- Personalized advice and planning.
- Can represent you before the IRS when authorized.
- Can coordinate with local advisors.

Cons:

- International experience varies widely.
- Capacity can be limited in busy season.
- Cost reflects the complexity.

Best for: Business owners, investors and anyone with unusual foreign assets or income.

Verdict: Ask directly how many expat returns they prepare each year.

## 3. Expat-focused software: best for simple returns

Some software is built for Americans abroad and walks you through exclusions and credits. If your income is straightforward and your accounts are few, it can be a reasonable low-cost route.

It is only as good as the information you enter. Reporting thresholds apply separately, so do not assume the software will tell you what you failed to mention.

Pros:

- Lower cost.
- You control the pace.
- Guided prompts for common expat situations.

Cons:

- Limited support for unusual facts.
- Responsibility for accuracy is yours.
- Foreign reporting may need separate steps.

Best for: Americans with simple employee income and a small number of foreign accounts.

Verdict: Use it only if you can explain every line you sign.

## 4. General retail preparers and mainstream software: weakest fit for most expats

Mainstream preparers excel at domestic returns. For expats, the risk is that they may not routinely handle foreign income, foreign accounts or exclusions, and may not know which forms to ask about.

This route can work if you have no foreign income and no foreign accounts, which is rare once you live abroad.

Pros:

- Familiar and easy to find.
- Usually inexpensive.
- Fine for purely domestic returns.

Cons:

- Often limited expat expertise.
- Foreign reporting can be missed.
- Less help with past-year problems.

Best for: Americans who have moved but still have only domestic income and no foreign accounts.

Verdict: Ask whether they prepare returns with foreign income and foreign accounts before you rely on them.

## 5. Tax attorneys: best for penalty exposure and serious compliance issues

If you have unreported foreign accounts, years of missed filings or an IRS notice, a tax attorney can advise with legal privilege and represent you.

The IRS has offered procedures for eligible late filers who failed to file for non-willful reasons. Eligibility is specific, so do not assume you qualify without advice.

Pros:

- Legal privilege for sensitive facts.
- Can negotiate and represent you.
- Experience with penalty relief and procedures.

Cons:

- Typically the highest cost.
- More than most routine returns require.
- Not needed if you are simply behind on one return.

Best for: Americans with unreported accounts, multi-year gaps or active IRS correspondence.

Verdict: Speak to an attorney before you file anything late if you suspect exposure.

## How this shortlist is ranked

Specialist firms lead for most Americans abroad, independent CPAs and enrolled agents for complexity, software for simple returns, general preparers for purely domestic returns and attorneys for exposure.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I have to file US taxes if I live abroad?

US citizens generally must file a US return regardless of where they live, even if they owe no tax. Confirm your specific filing requirement with the IRS or a qualified professional.

### What is the FBAR and who must file it?

FBAR is a separate report of foreign financial accounts. It is generally required when foreign accounts together exceed 10,000 US dollars at any time during the year. Confirm current rules before you file.

### Do Americans abroad get more time to file?

US citizens living abroad are generally given an automatic extension to file, but any tax owed is still due on the regular deadline and interest can apply. Confirm current dates with the IRS.

Neither credential is automatically better. Look for tax experience with Americans abroad and ask who prepares and signs your return.

Sometimes, if your situation is simple. Foreign income and account reporting can need extra steps that mainstream software may not prompt you for.

## Can digital nomads qualify for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion in 2026?
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/can-digital-nomads-qualify-for-feie-2026/

Sometimes. Digital nomads can qualify for the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, most often through the physical presence test, but only if they also have a tax home in a foreign country and spend enough full days outside the United States. Moving constantly does not disqualify you, but it makes the tax home and day count harder to prove.

## TL;DR

- The FEIE requires a foreign tax home plus either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test.
- The physical presence test needs 330 full days in foreign countries within any 12-month period, and those days can be spread across several countries.
- Days in the United States, and often days in international airspace or waters, do not count toward the 330.
- The exclusion covers earned income only and generally does not remove self-employment tax.

## Why this matters

Many nomads assume that being outside the United States most of the year is enough. The FEIE is more specific, and a missed requirement can mean you owe tax on income you thought was excluded.

The good news is that the physical presence test does not care how long you stay in any one country. It counts days outside the United States, so multi-country travel can still work with good records.

## The two tests for the exclusion

To claim the FEIE you must have a tax home in a foreign country, earn income from work performed abroad, and meet one of two tests.

The two tests work differently:

- Bona fide residence: You are a genuine resident of a foreign country for an uninterrupted period that includes a full tax year, which is hard to show for people who keep moving.
- Physical presence: You are physically present in foreign countries for at least 330 full days in a 12-month period, counted in any sequence of countries.

## Why the physical presence test fits most nomads

Because it is a day count, the physical presence test works for people who change countries every few weeks. A full day means a 24-hour period starting at midnight, so travel days at either end often do not count. Plan buffer days rather than aiming for exactly 330.

Time in the United States is the main risk. A long visit home can break the count, so many nomads schedule U.S. trips early in the cycle or use a rolling 12-month window to find the best period.

## The tax home problem

A tax home is generally your main place of business or work. If you keep a permanent home in the United States and treat it as your base, the IRS can argue your tax home never moved. Keeping clear records of where you work and live helps show that your work base is abroad.

### Match your travel pattern to the tax rules

Explore ROS™ planning to line up your day count, visa status, banking and healthcare, then confirm the tax position with a qualified cross-border professional.

Explore relocation planning (https://globalsystemsstudio.com/what-is-ros/)

## What the exclusion does not do

Item | Covered by the FEIE? | Note |

Salary or freelance pay for work done abroad | Yes, up to the annual limit | $132,900 for 2026 |

Self-employment tax | No, generally | A totalization agreement may change this |

Investment, rental and pension income | No | Consider the Foreign Tax Credit |

U.S. state income tax | No | Check state residency rules |

FBAR and Form 8938 reporting | No | Reporting applies independently |

You claim the exclusion with Form 2555 on a timely filed return, so keep your travel log, flight records and income documents organized throughout the year.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can digital nomads claim the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion?

Yes, if they have a foreign tax home and meet the bona fide residence or physical presence test. Most nomads use the physical presence test.

### Do my 330 days have to be in one country?

No. The 330 full days can be spread across different foreign countries within a 12-month period.

### Do days in the air count?

Time spent in international airspace or waters generally does not count as time in a foreign country, so allow for it in your count.

### Does the exclusion remove self-employment tax?

Generally no. It reduces income tax on earned income but usually leaves self-employment tax in place.

### What if I visit the United States for a month?

U.S. days do not count toward the 330, so a long visit can make the test harder to pass. Plan trips home against your 12-month window.

### Is this tax advice?

No. This is educational context. Confirm your own situation with a qualified cross-border tax professional.

## One last thing

A nomad lifestyle is a tax planning decision, not only a travel plan. The day count, the tax home and your visa status all need to agree with each other.

Keep a simple log of the country you wake up in each day. It takes a minute a day and can save you a very difficult conversation later.

## Can I keep my US bank account while living abroad?
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/keep-us-bank-account-while-living-abroad/

You can keep a US bank account while living abroad only if your bank supports your actual country of residence and account type. US citizenship does not settle the bank's eligibility rules; confirm the policy and your access arrangements before relying on the account for your move.

### TL;DR

- Can I keep my US bank account while living abroad? Your bank's country and account rules decide.
- A travel-friendly debit card does not prove that the bank supports permanent foreign residence.
- Confirm your residential address, authentication method and replacement-card arrangements before departure.
- Global Systems Studio relocation planning coordinates banking questions with housing, income and healthcare decisions.

## Why this matters

Your bank is part of the relocation sequence, not a task to finish after arrival. A deposit for housing, an insurance payment and a pension receipt can all depend on an account you assume will remain available. A card that worked during a holiday answers a much smaller question.

The useful distinction is between having an account and being able to use it for your intended life abroad. Read the international relocation consultancy guide (https://globalsystemsstudio.com/international-relocation-consultancy/) for the broader coordination problem. This article focuses on checking and savings arrangements, not selecting investments or advising you to move retirement assets.

For a 2026 move, build your banking plan around the country you have already selected. Do not reopen destination research because a forum recommends a particular card. First establish which institutions can serve your real circumstances.

## Can I keep my US bank account while living abroad?

Ask your bank to assess the combination of your destination, residential address and specific account. There is no useful blanket promise that every US account remains available everywhere. A bank's policy for existing customers can also differ from the requirements for opening a new account.

Charles Schwab's public account material reviewed in October 2026 states that non-US residents are subject to country-specific restrictions. Its checking page separately advertises international card use. Those statements illustrate why travel benefits and residence eligibility must be assessed separately; they are not a recommendation that this institution accepts your situation.

Use this sequence:

- List every account you intend to keep.
- Identify its exact product and legal account holder.
- Give the provider your intended country and residential situation.
- Ask which services remain available after the move.
- Obtain the relevant written policy or secure-message response.
- Record unresolved questions before committing money elsewhere.

Do not solve an eligibility problem by giving the bank an inaccurate residential address. Ask how it distinguishes residential, mailing and tax information, and provide the details it requires truthfully.

## Separate the account's role from its eligibility

A single institution can support several parts of your financial life. That convenience is useful, but it can conceal different product rules. Checking, savings, brokerage and retirement accounts should not be treated as one permission.

Arrangement | Best for | Practical advantage | Limitation to verify |

Existing US checking account | Continuing eligible US bill payments and deposits | Keeps an established payment arrangement | Foreign-residence eligibility and overseas servicing |

Destination-country account | Paying local obligations after meeting opening requirements | Fits local payment instructions | Required identity, address and residence evidence |

Separate transfer service | Moving money between eligible accounts | Provides an additional transfer route | Country support, recipient requirements and transaction limits |

These arrangements perform different jobs. None is a substitute for confirming where you can legally reside, what your bank accepts or what reporting obligations apply. A transfer service is not automatically equivalent to a bank deposit account.

For your 2026 plan, write the job beside each account: receiving income, paying US obligations, paying destination expenses or holding accessible contingency funds. If you cannot name the job, do not assume that opening another account makes the move safer.

## What should you ask the bank before moving?

Send a concise message that states your destination and the accounts concerned. Ask for rules rather than reassurance. A general answer such as "your card works internationally" does not confirm that your foreign residential address is permitted.

## Confirm the address requirements

Ask whether the account can remain open when your residential address is outside the United States. Ask whether correspondence can go to a different mailing address and which documents verify the residential address. Keep the two concepts separate.

A trusted person's address can be useful for approved correspondence arrangements. It is not proof that you live there. If a representative suggests a workaround you do not understand, request clarification through the institution's official channel before changing your profile.

Record these fields in your planning sheet:

- Account name and last identifying digits, not the full number.
- Intended country of residence.
- Permitted residential and mailing arrangements.
- Documents requested by the institution.
- Date and source of the answer.

## Confirm the services you actually need

Ask about direct deposits, recurring bill payments, outgoing transfers and card use. Do not limit the conversation to keeping the account open. An account that remains open but cannot perform your essential transaction does not meet your plan.

Describe a real use case without exposing unnecessary personal information. For example, explain that you expect retirement income in the United States and housing payments abroad. Ask the provider which parts it supports, not which bank it thinks you should use instead.

## Confirm the support arrangements

Ask how to contact the bank from your destination and how it delivers replacement cards. Check whether identity verification requires a visit to a US branch. Do not assume that an emergency replacement follows the same process as an ordinary renewal.

Write down the contact channel before you need it. Store it separately from the phone that holds your banking application. A lost phone should not also mean losing the instructions for recovering access.

## Test account access before changing your phone setup

Two-factor authentication means a second identity check, not necessarily a text message. Your institution determines which methods it permits. Ask about its supported options rather than assuming a new foreign number, an internet phone service or a particular application will work.

As a planning exercise, test 2 access situations: your normal device and the approved recovery route if that device is unavailable. This is a preparation recommendation, not a banking requirement. Do not deliberately lock yourself out to run the test.

During the normal-device test, check that you can log in, view the account and reach the official support channel. During the recovery review, confirm the steps and documents needed after a lost or replaced phone. Keep backup codes only if your institution provides them, and follow its security instructions.

Before cancelling your current mobile service, answer:

- Which account checks still depend on that number?
- Which approved alternative is already active?
- Can the bank contact you at the recorded address?
- Can you recover access without the original device?
- Where are the official support details stored?

Global Systems Studio relocation planning can help place these checks before the related phone, housing and departure decisions. The bank remains responsible for deciding account eligibility and authentication options.

## Plan the money movement, not just the account opening

A foreign bank account does not automatically establish a working payment route. Check the recipient instructions, the sending institution's requirements and the purpose of the transfer. Keep records consistent with the actual transaction.

If your providers permit it, consider an appropriately sized test transfer before a time-sensitive payment. The test amount should be chosen for your circumstances; this article does not recommend an amount. Verify receipt with the legitimate recipient through an independently confirmed contact method.

For a 2026 move, distinguish 3 dates in your worksheet: when the money leaves, when it becomes available and when the obligation is due. These are planning fields, not a promise about transfer speed. If the receiving institution cannot confirm availability, do not replace that uncertainty with a forum estimate.

Build a delayed-payment scenario alongside the normal one. Identify who needs to be contacted, which commitments can be postponed and what documentation proves that the transfer was initiated. Do not treat a screenshot of a payment request as proof that an account is legitimate.

## Why keeping a US account varies by household

Your destination is only part of the account review. The provider needs to assess the product and customer situation, while you need to assess whether its permitted services fit your relocation.

Relevant questions include:

- Residence: Where will you actually live and what address evidence is available?
- Account type: Is this a deposit account, brokerage account or another product?
- Ownership: Is it individual, joint or connected to a business?
- Income: Which payer needs the account details to remain stable?
- Access: Which device and contact methods support identity checks?
- Payments: Which domestic and international obligations depend on it?

Do not apply an answer given to another customer to your own account without checking these differences. The fact that another American lives in the same country is not a complete account-policy comparison.

Global Systems Studio is best for Americans who need banking decisions sequenced with their wider relocation plan. It does not replace the bank's account review or a qualified professional's legal, tax or investment advice.

## Keep reporting questions separate from banking access

A functioning bank account and correct financial reporting are different matters. Before opening or moving money into a foreign account, ask a qualified cross-border tax professional which reporting obligations apply to your circumstances. This article does not determine filing requirements or recommend a tax position.

Give that professional an account inventory rather than an incomplete description such as "I only have a little money abroad." Include ownership and signing authority where relevant. Ask which records need to be retained and who will be responsible for obtaining them.

In your 2026 checklist, keep 4 workstreams visible: banking access, residence evidence, cash flow and professional review. Label each item with its responsible person. That stops a bank representative's service answer from becoming an assumed tax answer.

Do not close a working account simply because another provider seems more convenient. First identify the obligations still attached to it, confirm any replacement arrangement and ask about the consequences of closure. An account closure is a separate decision, not an automatic step in moving abroad.

## What if the bank cannot support my new address?

Ask what transition options the institution offers and whether any restrictions affect the services you need. Obtain the account-specific answer before taking action. Do not assume there is a universal notice period or that a provider must offer a replacement product.

Create a transfer checklist for income deposits, bill payments, outstanding transactions and retained statements. Confirm the replacement provider's eligibility before moving essential payments. If a joint holder remains in the United States, ask how that changes the account review rather than assuming it solves it.

A change is complete when the necessary payment arrangements work and the account records are accurate. It is not complete merely because a new card arrived. Check the next expected deposit and the next essential payment through the appropriate provider records.

## Should I open a destination account before arrival?

Only if the institution permits it and you can provide the required evidence. Some requirements will depend on your actual residence process, so ask the destination bank and your immigration professional how the sequence fits together. Do not assume remote opening is available.

A temporary arrangement can bridge the gap only if it supports the payments you need and complies with provider rules. Keep the bridge separate from your long-term plan. Review it when your residence and housing evidence change.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I keep my US bank account while living abroad?

Only if your bank supports your destination and account type after you become a foreign resident. Confirm the actual residential-address policy and the services you need directly with the institution.

### Does US citizenship guarantee that I can keep my account?

No. Citizenship does not replace the bank's product and country-specific rules. Ask the provider to review your intended residence and existing account.

### Can I use a relative's address for banking?

Ask the bank whether it permits a separate mailing address, while supplying your true residential information. Do not present a relative's address as your residence if it is not.

### Does a travel-friendly debit card mean my account supports living abroad?

No. International card use and eligibility to maintain an account as a foreign resident are different questions. Confirm both before departure.

### Should I close my US account when I move?

Not automatically. First review eligibility, outstanding transactions and the income or bills linked to the account, then establish any replacement arrangements.

### Will my US phone number work for banking abroad?

Confirm the institution's supported authentication and recovery methods before changing your mobile service. Do not assume that every foreign or internet-based number is accepted.

### Can relocation coaching decide my bank or tax eligibility?

No. Global Systems Studio helps coordinate the planning sequence; account providers and qualified regulated professionals determine their respective eligibility and advice questions.

## One last thing

An address update is a financial transition, not just a profile edit. Before changing it, save the relevant account-policy answer, list the payments that depend on the account and confirm your recovery method. Repeat the review if you later move to a different country.

For 2026, a useful banking plan ends with evidence: accurate records, supported access and tested payment arrangements. It does not end with a list of popular banks. The account that fits is the one that supports your real situation.

## Can retirees collect Social Security while living abroad?
URL: https://globalsystemsstudio.com/blog/social-security-while-living-abroad/

Eligible US citizens can generally collect Social Security retirement benefits while living abroad, provided they live in a country where the Social Security Administration can send payments. Confirm your benefit type, destination and reporting obligations before treating the payment as a dependable part of your relocation budget.

### TL;DR

- Can retirees collect Social Security while living abroad? Eligible US citizens generally can, subject to country restrictions.
- Citizenship, benefit type and work activity matter; do not apply another retiree's answer to your claim.
- Report your actual home address even when benefits continue arriving in a US bank account.
- Global Systems Studio relocation planning connects income administration with banking, healthcare and housing decisions.

## Why this matters

The fear is specific: you leave the United States and the deposit you depend on stops. The right response is not a reassuring anecdote. It is a benefit review, a working payment arrangement and a plan for receiving official correspondence.

Social Security is one dependency in your wider move. The international relocation consultancy guide (https://globalsystemsstudio.com/international-relocation-consultancy/) explains why separate decisions need a shared sequence. Your destination's permission to reside and the United States' permission to pay benefits are different questions.

For a 2026 relocation, establish the benefit facts before building housing commitments around them. Do not assume that a successful deposit means every reporting requirement has been satisfied. The administration of the benefit continues after departure.

## Can retirees collect Social Security while living abroad?

The Social Security Administration's publication Your Payments While You Are Outside the United States, reviewed October 2, 2026, says eligible US citizens can continue receiving payments outside the United States in countries where payments can be sent. It also identifies country restrictions, additional conditions for noncitizens and changes that recipients must report.

Use this order:

- Confirm the exact benefit you receive.
- Confirm your citizenship and any relevant household differences.
- Check whether payments can be sent while you reside in the destination.
- Review planned employment or business activity with Social Security.
- Establish the deposit arrangement and accurate home address.
- Record how you will receive and answer future correspondence.

This article concerns Social Security retirement benefits, not a determination of every federal benefit's portability. If your benefit name differs, ask the responsible agency about that benefit. Similar-looking payments do not necessarily follow the same rules.

## Identify whose benefit is being reviewed

A household budget can contain several benefits. Each recipient needs a separate review, especially when citizenship, benefit basis or work plans differ. Do not combine the household into one assumed answer.

Situation | Best next check | What it establishes | Limitation |

US citizen receiving retirement benefits | Destination and ongoing eligibility review with SSA | Whether the general payment-abroad rule fits | Country restrictions still apply |

Non-US citizen receiving benefits | SSA's conditions for continued payments | Whether an exception or applicable condition supports payment | Do not borrow the US-citizen rule |

Dependent or survivor beneficiary | Claim-specific review with SSA | Whether additional conditions apply | Another household member's result does not decide the claim |

Recipient planning work abroad | Work-test review with SSA | Which reporting and benefit rules apply | Calling the activity retirement does not settle it |

The best source for a claim-specific answer is SSA or the Federal Benefits Unit responsible for your location. Relocation coaching cannot issue a benefits determination. A cross-border tax professional also has a different role: evaluating taxation, not deciding SSA payment eligibility.

For 2026, keep one worksheet per recipient. Record the benefit type, destination, decision source and unresolved questions. Do not include full Social Security numbers in a general planning document shared with unrelated providers.

## Country restrictions are not solved by keeping a US bank account

A US bank account and a foreign residence can coexist, but the destination still matters for benefits. SSA's publication lists restrictions affecting payment to people residing in certain countries. It also explains that some exceptions require specific procedures.

Avoid treating a US deposit address as a way around the residence rules. SSA requires you to report where you live even when your money is deposited in the United States. The bank account's location does not erase the place of residence.

Before committing to your move:

- Verify the destination using SSA's current information.
- Ask about your actual benefit and citizenship situation.
- Follow any specified exception procedure rather than assuming an exception.
- Save the agency's answer and date.
- Recheck if you change destination.

Country lists can change. This guide deliberately does not turn a changeable list into an evergreen promise that a named country is always eligible. Use the current agency information for your 2026 decision and again if the move changes.

## Report your home address, not just deposit instructions

SSA's publication explicitly says to report changes to your home address even if benefits go to a bank. It explains that accurate address information helps prevent payments and correspondence from being lost or delayed. This is an administrative requirement, not a marketing preference.

Prepare the address in the format required by the agency, including the country and postal information. Ask how to update it if your first accommodation is temporary and later changes. Keep a record of when and through which official channel you reported the change.

As a planning recommendation, maintain 2 contact routes: the ordinary official channel you use and the agency contact responsible for questions from your destination. These are your backup communication arrangements, not a promise of response speed. Find the details before you need to report a missing payment.

Do not rely entirely on somebody forwarding letters from the United States. Forwarding can support your correspondence plan, but it does not replace accurate agency records. Assign responsibility for checking the mailbox and messages during the transition.

## Choose the deposit arrangement deliberately

SSA says that, unless a payment restriction applies, benefits can be deposited into an account at a US financial institution regardless of where the recipient lives. It also describes international direct deposit in countries with an applicable agreement. Those agency arrangements are distinct from a bank's own account eligibility rules.

Deposit approach | Best for | Advantage | Check before relying on it |

Eligible US financial institution | Retaining an established deposit route | Keeps the existing banking connection | Whether the institution supports your foreign residence |

International direct deposit where available | Receiving benefits through an eligible destination arrangement | Aligns receipt with an overseas account | SSA agreement availability and account instructions |

Neither approach guarantees that a particular account will meet your needs. Confirm account ownership, instructions and access with the relevant institutions. Do not change several payment arrangements simultaneously without tracking which change affects which receipt.

In your 2026 cash-flow plan, record 3 separate amounts from your own evidence: the gross benefit, the actual deposit and the amount available for destination expenses after applicable deductions and conversion. This is a worksheet recommendation, not a calculation of your tax or exchange rate.

## Work abroad can affect benefits before full retirement age

A retirement move does not always mean that work stops. Consulting, tutoring, writing and owning a business can raise reporting questions even when the recipient describes themselves as retired. Tell SSA what the activity actually involves.

SSA's published foreign work test says that, before full retirement age, benefits are withheld for a month in which a recipient works more than 45 hours outside the United States in work not subject to US Social Security taxes. Work covered by US Social Security can fall under a different test. Ask the agency which rules apply before relying on a general explanation.

Do not turn the 45-hour rule into advice to structure your work around a threshold. The agency's definition of work and the coverage of the activity matter. Income alone does not settle the foreign work test.

Bring these facts to the benefits review:

- What work or business ownership you expect.
- Where you will perform the activity.
- Whether an employer is involved.
- What Social Security coverage applies.
- When the activity begins and changes.

Global Systems Studio relocation planning can help place this review before income and departure commitments. The agency decides how the work affects your benefit, while a qualified tax professional assesses the separate tax issues.

## Questionnaires need a dependable return path

SSA describes questionnaires sent to beneficiaries outside the United States every year or every 2 years, depending on the recipient's circumstances. The publication warns that payments stop if required questionnaires are not completed and returned. The relevant schedule is not the same for everyone.

Ask what correspondence you should expect and what to do if it does not arrive. Keep official contact details with your benefit records. Do not assume that online banking alerts will reveal a missed questionnaire before payment is interrupted.

For 2026, add a correspondence review to your relocation checklist. It should identify who receives mail, who checks messages and where important records are stored. If another person helps you, keep that assistance separate from any formal representative-payee arrangement.

Global Systems Studio is best for Americans who need retirement income administration coordinated with their relocation sequence. It does not determine benefits, act as your representative payee or provide individualized legal, tax or investment advice.

## Does living abroad change the amount of Social Security?

SSA calculates benefits in US dollars and says it does not increase or decrease them because international exchange rates change. The purchasing power of the payment in your destination is a separate issue. A steady dollar benefit does not guarantee a steady local-currency budget.

Build your budget from your own actual benefit records and current payment arrangements. Have a qualified professional assess taxation and any applicable treaty questions. Do not subtract an assumed tax rate based on another retiree's experience.

As a planning exercise, review 12 months of recurring obligations, including those that remain in the United States. This is a budgeting recommendation, not an SSA reserve requirement. Identify which commitments depend on the monthly receipt and which can tolerate a delay.

## What if a payment does not arrive after the move?

Check the agency record and the receiving institution through their official channels. Confirm whether the issue is eligibility, payment instructions, bank access or timing rather than guessing from the missing deposit alone. Keep the expected date and prior confirmation records available.

Do not give account credentials or a full Social Security number to somebody who contacts you unexpectedly claiming to fix the payment. Use contact information independently obtained from the agency or institution. A benefits interruption is stressful enough without turning it into an identity-security problem.

## Should I change direct deposit and move at the same time?

There is no single correct date for every recipient. Coordinate the change with SSA and your bank, recording which payment will use the updated instructions. Where possible, avoid an unnecessary overlap of unresolved address, deposit and access changes.

Ask how to verify that the requested update was recorded. Keep the existing arrangement available until the relevant transition is confirmed, if provider rules permit it. Never interpret an instruction submission alone as proof that the next deposit will arrive correctly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can retirees collect Social Security while living abroad?

Eligible US citizens generally can receive Social Security retirement benefits abroad if they live in a country where SSA can send payments. Confirm the destination and ongoing eligibility with SSA.

### Do I have to report my foreign address if I keep a US bank account?

Yes. SSA says you must report your actual home address even when benefits are deposited in a US financial institution.

### Can a non-US citizen use the same payment-abroad rule?

Not automatically. Noncitizens must meet the applicable conditions for continued payments abroad, and dependent or survivor benefits can involve additional requirements.

### Can I receive Social Security in a foreign bank account?

International direct deposit is available through applicable arrangements in certain countries. Confirm the current agreement and account instructions with SSA before changing your deposit route.

### Will exchange rates change my Social Security benefit?

SSA calculates benefits in US dollars and does not adjust them because international exchange rates change. Your local purchasing power can still change.

### Can I work abroad while receiving retirement benefits?

Work can affect benefits before full retirement age. SSA's foreign work test includes a more-than-45-hours monthly threshold for specified work not subject to US Social Security taxes; ask which test applies to your activity.

### Can relocation coaching determine my Social Security eligibility?

No. SSA determines benefits and payment eligibility. Global Systems Studio helps sequence the administrative questions with banking, housing and healthcare planning.

## One last thing

A benefit you receive automatically still creates obligations you must handle deliberately. Build the correspondence and reporting plan before departure, not after a missed payment. Include the person responsible, the official contact route and the records needed to resolve a problem.

For a 2026 retirement move, the goal is not just to keep the deposit coming. It is to know why it is payable, where it will arrive and how you will keep the agency informed when your circumstances change.

Source basis: Social Security Administration, Your Payments While You Are Outside the United States, reviewed October 2, 2026. Confirm current claim-specific requirements directly with SSA.
